title: Does exercise actually relate to fitness?
text:
For this post I wanted to try a small sports/fitness dataset in Python. I picked one that’s built right into scikit-learn called linnerud. It has data from 20 middle-aged men who did 3 exercises (chin-ups, sit-ups, and jumps) and also had 3 physical measurements taken (weight, waist, and pulse). I wanted to see if doing more of these exercises is actually related to having a lower weight, smaller waist, or lower pulse.
Source: linnerud dataset, built into scikit-learn.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_linnerud

title: Does exercise actually relate to fitness?
text:
For this post I wanted to try a small sports/fitness dataset in Python. I picked one that’s built right into scikit-learn called linnerud. It has data from 20 middle-aged men who did 3 exercises (chin-ups, sit-ups, and jumps) and also had 3 physical measurements taken (weight, waist, and pulse). I wanted to see if doing more of these exercises is actually related to having a lower weight, smaller waist, or lower pulse.
Source: linnerud dataset, built into scikit-learn.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_linnerud

title: Does exercise actually relate to fitness?
text:
Loading the data
The dataset comes split into two parts: the exercise numbers and the physical measurements. I put them together into one table so it’s easier to work with.

linnerud = load_linnerud()

exercise = pd.DataFrame(linnerud.data, columns=linnerud.feature_names)
physio = pd.DataFrame(linnerud.target, columns=linnerud.target_names)

data = pd.concat([exercise, physio], axis=1)

Looking at the averages, people did about 9-10 chin-ups, 145 sit-ups, and 70 jumps on average, and had an average waist size of about 35 inches and pulse of about 56.

title: Does exercise actually relate to fitness?
text:
Chin-ups vs waist size
My first guess was that people who can do more chin-ups probably have a smaller waist. I made a scatter plot to check this.

plt.scatter(data["Chins"], data["Waist"])
plt.xlabel("Chin-ups")
plt.ylabel("Waist (inches)")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Chin-ups vs waist size for 20 men.





There does seem to be a slight downward pattern here, so people who could do more chin-ups tended to have a somewhat smaller waist, but it’s not a super strong relationship and there are some exceptions.

title: Does exercise actually relate to fitness?
text:
Sit-ups vs pulse
Next I checked if people who did more sit-ups had a lower resting pulse.

plt.scatter(data["Situps"], data["Pulse"])
plt.xlabel("Sit-ups")
plt.ylabel("Pulse")
plt.show()







Figure 2: Sit-ups vs pulse for 20 men.





This one doesn’t look like it has much of a pattern at all. The points are pretty scattered, so based on this small dataset, sit-ups don’t seem to be clearly related to pulse.

title: Does exercise actually relate to fitness?
text:
Conclusion
Using the linnerud dataset, I found a moderate relationship between chin-ups and waist size, but almost no relationship between sit-ups and pulse. This dataset is very small (only 20 people), so I wouldn’t take these results too seriously, but it was a good first try at loading a built-in dataset and making some plots in Python.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation was three days of meeting new people, alumni, faculty, and honestly way too much information to absorb at once. The best part was a scavenger hunt style activity where we roamed campus in groups, finding spots and completing little tasks together. It was a solid way to actually learn my way around while getting to know my cohort.
Then classes started, and the pace jumped fast. Four subjects running at once means four new sets of concepts to wrap my head around every single week.
Each course has a worksheet and lab due by week’s end, so the routine is already forming. Learn, apply, submit, repeat. Two weeks in and it’s intense, but the good kind of intense.

title: Who tackles the most? Looking at 2010 World Cup player stats
text:
For this post I wanted to look at some football data and see if I could find anything interesting using R. I always assumed defenders do most of the tackling on a team, so I decided to check if that is actually true using real player data from the 2010 World Cup.
I’m using the worldcup dataset that comes with the faraway R package. It has stats for 595 players from the 2010 World Cup, like their position, minutes played, tackles, shots, passes, and saves.
Source: worldcup dataset from the faraway package.

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(faraway)

title: Who tackles the most? Looking at 2010 World Cup player stats
text:
For this post I wanted to look at some football data and see if I could find anything interesting using R. I always assumed defenders do most of the tackling on a team, so I decided to check if that is actually true using real player data from the 2010 World Cup.
I’m using the worldcup dataset that comes with the faraway R package. It has stats for 595 players from the 2010 World Cup, like their position, minutes played, tackles, shots, passes, and saves.
Source: worldcup dataset from the faraway package.

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(faraway)

title: Who tackles the most? Looking at 2010 World Cup player stats
text:
Looking at the data
First I just want to see what the data looks like.

head(worldcup)

               Team   Position Time Shots Passes Tackles Saves
Abdoun      Algeria Midfielder   16     0      6       0     0
Abe           Japan Midfielder  351     0    101      14     0
Abidal       France   Defender  180     0     91       6     0
Abou Diaby   France Midfielder  270     1    111       5     0
Aboubakar  Cameroon    Forward   46     2     16       0     0
Abreu       Uruguay    Forward   72     0     15       0     0


There are some players who barely played any minutes, which might mess up the results, so I decided to only keep players who played at least 10 minutes.

worldcup2 <- worldcup |>
  filter(Time >= 10)

nrow(worldcup2)

[1] 575

title: Who tackles the most? Looking at 2010 World Cup player stats
text:
Tackles by position
My main question was whether defenders really do tackle more than other positions. Since players play different amounts of time, I calculated tackles per 90 minutes so it’s a fair comparison.

worldcup2 <- worldcup2 |>
  mutate(tackles_per_90 = Tackles / Time * 90) |>
  filter(Position != "Goalkeeper")

worldcup2 |>
  group_by(Position) |>
  summarise(avg_tackles = round(mean(tackles_per_90), 2))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Position   avg_tackles
  <fct>            <dbl>
1 Defender          2.13
2 Forward           1.14
3 Midfielder        2.33


This table already shows defenders have the highest average tackles per 90 minutes, which is what I expected. I also made a plot to see this a bit more clearly.

worldcup2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Position, y = tackles_per_90)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(y = "Tackles per 90 minutes")







Figure 1: Tackles per 90 minutes for each position (goalkeepers not included).





Defenders clearly tackle the most on average, but there is also a lot of overlap between positions — some midfielders tackle just as much as some defenders.

title: Who tackles the most? Looking at 2010 World Cup player stats
text:
Shots vs passes
I was also curious if there’s a relationship between how many passes a player makes and how many shots they take, since I’d guess attackers pass less but shoot more.

worldcup2 |>
  filter(Position != "Goalkeeper") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Passes, y = Shots, color = Position)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Passes", y = "Shots")







Figure 2: Shots vs passes for each player, coloured by position.





This roughly matches what I expected — a lot of the points with more shots and fewer passes tend to be forwards, while defenders are usually on the other side with more passes and almost no shots.

title: Who tackles the most? Looking at 2010 World Cup player stats
text:
Conclusion
Using the worldcup dataset, I found that defenders do tackle the most on average compared to other positions, which confirms what I assumed at the start. The passes vs shots plot also lined up with what I expected — forwards shoot more and pass less, while defenders do the opposite. This was a good first practice at loading a dataset, cleaning it a bit, and making some plots in R.

title: About
text:
Background
I grew up in Delhi, India, and studied Electrical Engineering for my Bachelor’s. I then worked as a Data Engineer at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, building data pipelines in financial crime — working with data at scale and seeing how the right infrastructure can catch things that matter. That experience gave me a strong engineering foundation, but also pulled me toward the modeling and decision-making side of things, which led me to pursue a Master’s in Data Science.


Why Data Science
Working in financial crime showed me that the hard part isn’t moving data around — it’s making sense of it and building systems that act on it intelligently. I grew increasingly drawn to the machine learning side of the pipelines I built: how models are designed, trained, and deployed to catch patterns humans miss. That curiosity brought me to the MDS program at UBC, where I want to go deeper into the theory and practice of ML and build the skills to design models and systems myself, not just support the teams that do.


Outside of Data Science
Outside of data and models, I’m usually watching or playing football. Five-a-side on weekends, or a good match from the couch, or deep into a video game to switch off. I also love spending time with my fiancée, gaming and watching TV or movies together is one of our favorite things to do.
